rationale: A wins because it keeps the angles sharp and polices its own evidence. “Replit Built a Platform to Teach Coding. Now It's Selling a Tool That Skips It.” is the cleanest journalist-shaped tension in either set, and its proof list knows exactly what would make or break the story. B has real material, but “Replit's new agent lets non-coders spin up live databases. Who's checking what's in them?” stretches one database fact into a cybersecurity story before the evidence earns it. That is how a decent pitch walks itself into a reporter's follow-up buzzsaw.
gaps_in_A: “Replit Built a Platform to Teach Coding” slightly overstates the supplied facts; the update says Replit is a browser-based coding platform used heavily in education, not that it was built specifically to teach coding.
“replaces the development workflow for non-engineers entirely” is a little too absolute for a launch with undisclosed reliability. The proof section catches this, but the claim should be tightened.
The category angle needs a named market comparator before it becomes more than one company’s launch wearing a trend coat.
gaps_in_B: “a huge, largely non-technical user base” is not in the update. Replit has tens of millions of users and targets non-engineers with this agent; that does not prove its existing user base is largely non-technical.
“betting its core product on people who've never written code” invents company strategy. The update says it is launching an agent, not that it is betting the core product on this audience.
“Who's checking what's in them?” turns “sets up a database” into a shadow-IT/security angle without supplied evidence of enterprise use, misconfiguration, sensitive data, or guardrails failing.
“Now it can write the homework too” is catchy, but it edges toward academic-integrity inference. Usable with educator sourcing; too glib without it.
